rule: Sou says who you are, and é says who someone else is: both are forms of ser, to be. In Brazil, you is você, and it takes the same verb form as he and she: você é. Eu and você can be left out when the verb makes it clear: Sou um menino. Every noun is masculine or feminine: um goes with a masculine noun (um homem, um menino), uma with a feminine one (uma mulher, uma menina). To say not, put não before the verb: Eu não sou Tom. Não é? at the end of a sentence asks for agreement, like right?

Three ways to keep a conversation going. Não entendo means I don't understand, and Não entendi means I didn't catch that. Mais devagar asks for slower speech: Fale mais devagar, por favor. Pode repetir? asks someone to say it again; pode means can you, and the next verb stays in its dictionary form: Pode falar mais devagar? Por favor makes each one polite.

The word for the changes with the noun: o before a masculine noun (o livro), a before a feminine one (a casa). Brazilians often put it before a name too: o Tom, a Mary. Ele is he and ela is she. Esse and essa point at something: esse with a masculine noun, essa with a feminine one. Isso is that or this when no noun is named: Isso é um livro. An adjective in -o changes to -a with a feminine noun (pequeno, pequena); one in -e stays the same (grande, forte). A job has no um or uma: Ele é professor.

To ask how someone is, Portuguese uses estar, not ser: Como você está? and the answer is Estou bem. Como vai? and Tudo bem? ask the same thing. A man says obrigado and a woman says obrigada; the answer is De nada. Bom dia is for the morning, boa tarde for the afternoon and boa noite for the evening and at bedtime. Com licença gets someone's attention or asks to pass; desculpe says sorry.

A verb changes its ending with the person: como is I eat and come is he, she or you eat; bebo is I drink and bebe is he, she or you drink. Como also means how. To say what you like, use gostar with de: Eu gosto de leite, Você gosta de chá? The de is always there.

Ter means to have: tenho is I have, and tem is he, she or you have. Tem on its own also means there is or there are, which is how Brazilians usually say it: Tem leite? Não goes before the verb: Não tenho cachorro.

Two questions for words you don't know. Como se diz…? asks how something is said: Como se diz isso em português? O que significa…? and O que quer dizer…? both ask what a word means. Quer dizer is two words, wants to say, and together they mean means.

For more than one, most nouns add -s (livro, livros; maçã, maçãs). A noun in -m changes to -ns (homem, homens), and one in -r adds -es (mulher, mulheres). The word for the changes too: os for masculine plurals, as for feminine ones. An adjective follows: grande, grandes; bom, bons. Nós somos is we are; vocês são is you are, speaking to several people; eles and elas são is they are. Temos and têm are the same forms of ter.

An adjective agrees with its noun: novo, velho and bonito with a masculine noun, nova, velha and bonita with a feminine one. Bom becomes boa. Jovem doesn't change. Most adjectives come after the noun (um carro muito velho). Muito before an adjective means very; after a verb it means a lot. Também means also.

Gostar de can take a verb as well as a noun: Gosto de nadar means I like swimming. The verb stays in its dictionary form, ending in -ar or -er: nadar, dançar, cantar, ler. With a person the ending changes: canto is I sing and canta is he, she or you sing. Ler is irregular: leio is I read, lê is he, she or you read.

Estar says where someone or something is: está for one, estão for several, estamos for we. Em means in, on or at, and it joins with the word for the: em and o make no (no jardim, no banheiro), em and a make na (na cozinha, na cama). Em casa, with no the, means at home. Aqui is here and lá is there. Tem says what there is: Tem um gato na mesa.

How you feel right now takes estar. With an adjective, it agrees with the person: a man says Estou cansado, a woman Estou cansada; feliz, triste and doente don't change. Hunger, thirst, sleepiness, fear, cold and heat take estar com and a noun, where English says to be: Estou com fome is I'm hungry, Estou com sede I'm thirsty, Estou com sono I'm sleepy, Estou com frio I'm cold.

When the word won't come, say so and describe the thing. Estou procurando a palavra means I'm looking for the word. É uma coisa para… means it's a thing for…, followed by a verb: É uma coisa para ler. Como se chama isso? asks what something is called. Não sei means I don't know. Sabe with a verb asks whether someone knows how: Você sabe nadar?

My and your agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: meu and seu with a masculine noun, minha and sua with a feminine one, meus and minhas for the plurals. Seu and sua usually mean your in Brazil. For his and her, Brazilians put dele or dela after the noun: o pai dele is his father, a casa dela is her house.

Question words come first: quem (who), o que (what), onde (where), quando (when), qual (which) and por que (why). Que before a noun means what or which: Que livro é esse? Why is two words, por que; because is one word, porque, and it starts the answer: Por que você está triste? Porque estou cansado.

Onde fica…? asks where a place is; fica is used for places that don't move, and Onde é…? and Onde está…? are heard too. Perto means near and longe means far. Tem asks whether there is one: Tem um hospital aqui perto? De says how you travel: de trem, de ônibus.

The numbers from three to ten don't change. Two does: dois with a masculine noun, duas with a feminine one, like um and uma. How many is quantos with a masculine plural (quantos livros) and quantas with a feminine one (quantas maçãs). Age uses ter, to have: Quantos anos você tem? Tenho dez anos.

A colour comes after its noun and agrees with it: vermelho, preto, branco and amarelo with a masculine noun, vermelha, preta, branca and amarela with a feminine one. Azul and verde are the same for both. Que cor é…? asks what colour something is.

Hoje is today, amanhã tomorrow and agora now. The days of the week have no capital letter, and the weekdays end in -feira: segunda-feira, sexta-feira. Que dia é hoje? asks the day. The time is asked and told in the plural: Que horas são? São duas horas.

Ir, to go, is irregular: vou is I go, vai is he, she or you go, and vamos is we go, which also means let's go. To a place is para or a. A joins with the word for the: a and o make ao (ao parque), a and a make à, with its accent (à escola, à loja). Para keeps the word for the: para a escola.

To describe someone, use ter: Ela tem cabelo curto, she has short hair; Tenho olhos azuis, I have blue eyes. The adjective comes after the noun and agrees with it, so plural olhos take azuis and verdes. Alto and baixo describe a man, alta a woman. An ache is estar com dor: Estou com dor de cabeça is I have a headache. A pé means on foot.
